Consult Summary:
- Patient reported difficulty breathing and local rash minutes after an insect sting (bee/wasp) to the arm.
- Video assessment showed normal breathing and no visible oral/lip swelling; impression is a localized allergic reaction without anaphylaxis. Safety-netting and OTC antihistamine advised.

Problem List:

Issue 1:
- Localized reaction to insect sting (bee/wasp uncertain) to arm; onset: a few minutes before call.
- Symptoms: mild erythema and puncture mark at sting site; patient reported possible right-sided lip swelling and “tongue feels weird”; anxiety about breathing; no prior anaphylaxis, no EpiPen.
- Pertinent negatives: clinician observed no visible lip swelling; no stridor; patient did not feel acutely breathless during call.
- Examination (video): normal work of breathing; speaking in full sentences; oropharynx and lips appear without swelling; arm with mild erythema and puncture mark, no clear swelling.
- Impression: localized allergic reaction; no current features of anaphylaxis. Advised red flags and escalation.

Issue 2:
- Anxiety related to acute sting and fear of allergic reaction.
- History of intermittent anxiety; no prior medication.
- Management: reassurance; education on warning signs; advised low threshold to re-contact if worried.

Issue 3:
- History of eczema; no current treatment discussed; stable.

Medications:
- None reported as current.
- Antihistamine recommended: chlorphenamine (Piriton) 4 mg tablet PO, up to six times daily (OTC). Alternative “one-a-day” antihistamine option mentioned (dose/route/frequency not documented).

Allergies:
- Penicillin (reaction details not documented).

Past Medical History:
- Eczema.
- Intermittent anxiety (no medications).
- No history of anaphylaxis.

Social History:
- Lives alone.
- Occupation: computer scientist.
- Has a cat.
- Smoking and alcohol use not documented.

Preventative History:
- Not discussed.

Physical Examination:
- Vitals: not documented.
- Video exam: normal respiratory effort; no audible stridor; speaking in full sentences. Lips and oropharynx without visible swelling. Right arm: mild erythema with puncture mark; no obvious swelling.

Plan:
- Start OTC antihistamine as needed: chlorphenamine 4 mg up to six times daily, or a once-daily antihistamine alternative.
- Urgent ED care if any red flags: progressive lip/tongue/throat swelling, difficulty breathing, stridor, voice changes, or rapidly worsening symptoms.
- Re-assess if local redness spreads, becomes hot or painful, or systemic symptoms develop; may require antibiotics if signs of local infection occur.
- No immediate need for allergy testing or epinephrine auto-injector at this time; consider evaluation if reactions recur or become more severe.
- Patient information on anaphylaxis provided. Follow up with clinic if symptoms persist, worsen, or recur.

Quality checks:
● Missing expected elements: vitals; complete medication list and reconciliation; details of penicillin reaction; smoking and alcohol history; full review of systems; immunization status (including tetanus) not discussed.  
● Internal conflicts: Patient stated age as 27 but gave DOB as 1991-11-17 (conflict noted). Patient reported possible lip swelling/tongue symptoms; clinician observed no visible swelling (both statements documented). Insect type uncertain (bee vs wasp).  
● Transcript quality: Generally clear; minor transcription artifacts and filler, but clinical content understandable.
